title: introducing bob, the mtg ai ecosystem. v1.
author: Mean-Committee-4035
selftext:
[https://github.com/Bradsadevnow/bob](https://github.com/Bradsadevnow/bob)

What Bob is, and why it matters

Bob is not a chatbot wrapper and not a black-box agent. It is an AI runtime designed specifically for rules-driven environments where correctness, trust, and long-term improvement matter more than raw autonomy.

The system is structured around strict separation of concerns:

\- Authoritative truth lives only in deterministic engines like mtg\_core.

\- AI decision-making is constrained to player-scoped visible state and schema-defined legal actions.

\- Learning is explicit and auditable, never implicit or silent.

\-Memory is governed, with short-term continuity separated from long-term knowledge that requires human approval.



This allows Bob to learn from play and discussion without ever mutating game truth, leaking hidden information, or accumulating unchecked beliefs.



How learning works in practice



During gameplay, Bob operates strictly within the legal action schema produced by mtg\_core. Every decision, resolution, and outcome is logged deterministically. After or during play, Bob can engage in human discussion by answering questions, explaining why a play was legal, or reflecting on outcomes. From these interactions and from repeated gameplay patterns, Bob can propose learning candidates such as:



\-recurring strategic mistakes or improvements,

\- player preferences (pace, tutoring style, deck tendencies),

\- short, falsifiable lessons tied to specific archetypes or mechanics.



Crucially, Bob cannot commit these learnings on its own. All long-term memory writes are proposed, reviewed, edited if necessary, and explicitly approved by a human, with a permanent audit log. Game-specific hidden information and in-progress tactical details are never stored as durable knowledge. This creates a learning loop that is grounded in real gameplay, shaped by human feedback, safe against rules hallucination, and fully inspectable after the fact.



In live play, mtg\_core produces a player-visible snapshot of the game state. Bob uses this snapshot to enumerate a bounded schema of legal actions. The AI selects one action, submits it back to the engine, and mtg\_core validates and resolves it. The AI never mutates state directly. It never invents actions. It never sees hidden zones. All outcomes are deterministic and replayable.



This is not theoretical. I’ve already integrated the AI directly into the engine and implemented phase-1 Magic gameplay end-to-end: priority, stack resolution, mana and costs (including alternate and additional costs), combat, triggered and activated abilities, state-based actions, flashback, equipment, and dozens of card-specific effects.



What this enables for Magic players:



This ecosystem enables AI integration without compromising Magic’s integrity. AI opponents that improve over time while always playing legally. It enables teaching and tutoring systems that can explain decisions grounded in real game state. It creates debuggable learning where you can see why the AI changed its behavior. Just as importantly, the system is designed to fail safely. When something goes wrong, it’s visible, traceable, and correctable by humans.

comments.author: fisj
comments.body: This looks like a demo/project/workflow, not a commercial product. I'm changing the flair to match.

comments.author: Otherwise_Wave9374
comments.body:
This is a really nice example of "bounded agency" done right: deterministic engine as source of truth, agent only selects from a legal action schema, and all learning is auditable. That feels like the blueprint for a lot of real world agent systems (finance ops, infra changes, etc).

How are you thinking about evaluation, do you run self play tournaments, scenario suites, or regression tests over game logs?

Im always looking at similar agent architecture patterns, collecting some notes here: https://www.agentixlabs.com/blog/

replies.author: Mean-Committee-4035
replies.body: Thanks! Bounded agency is exactly the intent. I’ve been focusing on deterministic replay and scenario-based regression testing before leaning into self-play.

comments.author: hamsterofpuppets
comments.body: Hey  good work! Have you looked at all into [https://github.com/Card-Forge/forge](https://github.com/Card-Forge/forge) ? It's an open source rules engine and there's plenty of room there for integration with non-deterministic AI. Specifically it currently implements a classic branch-and-bound search algorithm but there might be ways to integrate LLM outputs into it. It'd save you time on the MTG game implementation end at the very least.

replies.author: Mean-Committee-4035
replies.body: I have, yeah. I looked at hijacking the forge AI, because with the utmost respect to the team behind forge that's more along the lines of monte carlo search than a full ai. however, because of the way that the ai needs to interact with the game and memory i just needed to rip it myself

replies.author: hamsterofpuppets
replies.body: Makes sense. I was more thinking of like, just use their game engine (so you don't have to worry about idk, implementing cards, rules, mtg game logic etc) and then just replace the AI module with yours if that makes sense?

replies.author: Mean-Committee-4035
replies.body: yeah, totally, and i considered it. it just didn't allow what i needed, and changing it, would have honestly been more work
